title: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
seo_title: Organic Chemistry Class 11 Chemistry Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 8)
standard_code: Class 11 Chemistry, Chapter 8: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
standard_text: General introduction, classification and IUPAC nomenclature of organic compounds. Electronic displacements in a covalent bond: inductive effect, electromeric effect, resonance and hyperconjugation. Homolytic and heterolytic fission of a covalent bond: free radicals, carbocations, carbanions, electrophiles and nucleophiles, types of organic reactions. Methods of purification, qualitative and quantitative analysis.
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 11 Chemistry worksheets for NCERT Chapter 8 Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques: hybridisation, functional groups, IUPAC names, isomerism, electrophiles and nucleophiles, and estimation of C, H, N and halogens. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Name by the longest chain, the main functional group and the lowest locants.
key_sub: Electrophiles seek electrons; nucleophiles give electron pairs.
body_html:
How to think about it

Carbon forms four bonds using sp³ (single bonds), sp² (one double bond) or sp (a triple bond or two double bonds) hybrids. Compounds are grouped by functional group and named by IUPAC rules. Isomers can differ in chain, position, functional group or metamerism.

Bonds break homolytically (free radicals) or heterolytically (carbocations and carbanions). Electrophiles such as H⁺ and NO₂⁺ accept electron pairs; nucleophiles such as OH⁻ and NH₃ donate them. Elements are estimated quantitatively: %C = (12/44) × m(CO₂)/m × 100, %H = (2/18) × m(H₂O)/m × 100, N by Kjeldahl's method and halogens by Carius method.

Example

Hybridisation of C in C₂H₂?

triple bond

Answer: sp

Example

0.2 g gives 0.44 g CO₂. %C?

12/44 × 0.44/0.2 × 100

Answer: 60%

Common mistakes

  • Calling NH₃ an electrophile.
  • Using 44/12 instead of 12/44 for % carbon.
  • Numbering a chain from the wrong end.

faq.q: How do you tell an electrophile from a nucleophile?
faq.a: An electrophile is electron-poor and accepts an electron pair; a nucleophile is electron-rich and donates one.

faq.q: Why is a tertiary carbocation the most stable?
faq.a: Three alkyl groups release electrons by inductive effect and hyperconjugation, spreading out the positive charge.
